title: Warm growing seasons did not increase size-standardised mercury in walleye, pike and lake trout in the same Ontario lakes (1970-2018), so warming does not explain the post-1995 rise
abstract: Question: after about 1995, size-standardised mercury (Hg) in Ontario predatory fish increased again, mostly in the north. Many authors suggest climate warming as the cause. We tested whether warm growing seasons increase Hg in fish of the same length in the same lake. Data: Ontario MECP Fish Contaminant Data, 1970-2018 (walleye, northern pike, lake trout; skinless dorsal fillet; 6,067 sampling events, 86,416 fish, 2,223 waterbodies); a CC0 Minnesota subset, 2000-2023 (1,126 events) as an independent region; Berkeley Earth 1-degree May-Sep air temperature. Method: each fish was moved to a standard length with lake-specific within-event length slopes. Event log Hg was regressed on the mean anomaly of the three last growing seasons, with lake-species and species-year fixed effects. Intervals are clustered by lake and year. Controls: placebo future seasons, a field-swap null, sub-periods, species, zones, weighting and standardisation variants. We compared observed 1995-2018 within-lake trends with the trend that local warming implies, and did a cross-lake trend test. Results: the post-1995 increase is present to 2018 (walleye north +7.4% per decade, 95% CI +3.0 to +11.9; lake trout south +14.7%, +4.0 to +26.5). In the same lakes, +1 C of growing-season temperature changed Hg by -6.8% (-14.6 to +1.8). All Ontario variants had negative point estimates (upper limits at most +8.7%). The placebo gave +2.9% (-4.7 to +11.1). Warming of 0.20-0.38 C per decade implies -1.4% to -2.6% per decade (at most +0.7%). Series with more local warming had smaller increases (slope -0.14, SE 0.06). Temperature did not change fish condition. Minnesota gave -9.9% (-40.9 to +37.2); this test has low power. Conclusion: in Ontario, growing-season warmth did not increase size-standardised fish Hg, and regional warming cannot explain the post-1995 increase. Other causes (food webs, invasive species, organic carbon, water levels, sampling changes) remain open. Limitations: air temperature at 1 degree is a proxy for lake temperature; interannual effects can differ from slow decadal effects; lakes are not a random sample; pre-1984 sampling dates are often only years; Minnesota is a selected subset with low power.

display.caption: Change in size-standardised fish Hg per +1 C of the mean May-Sep air temperature anomaly of the last three growing seasons. All models have lake-species fixed effects; the main models also have species-year fixed effects. Bars are 95% intervals clustered by lake and year. Grey: placebo with seasons 2-4 years after sampling. Purple: Minnesota (2000-2023, low power).

Left: observed within-lake Hg trends (% per decade, 95% CI) in 1995-2018 (Ontario, north and south of 47 N) and 2000-2023 (Minnesota), next to the trend that local warming multiplied by the main temperature slope implies (error bars use the slope CI). Right: own Hg trend of 238 Ontario lake-species series against own local warming; the line is the least-squares fit (negative).

Size-standardised Hg year effects inside lake-species series (dots, size = number of events; lines = 5-year event-weighted means) for Ontario north and south of 47 N and for Minnesota, with May-Sep air temperature anomalies (Berkeley Earth) at the sampled cells below. The grey band marks 1995-2018.

citations.reason: Thomas, Melles and Bhavsar (2018) found that growth dilution with latitude-zone warming did not explain Ontario walleye and pike Hg trends; our direct within-lake temperature test agrees that warming does not explain them.
Minnesota fish Hg subset (CC0) used as the independent region.
